output.query: acute rheumatic fever carditis atrioventricular block diagnosis, pacing and secondary prophylaxis

results.key_finding: Separate criteria for low-risk and moderate/high-risk populations. In moderate/high-risk populations polyarthralgia counts as a major manifestation; fever of 38.0 C or more, ESR of 30 mm/h or more and/or CRP of 3.0 mg/dL or more, and a prolonged PR interval for age (unless carditis is counted as a major criterion) are minor manifestations. A recurrence in a patient with prior rheumatic fever or rheumatic heart disease is diagnosed with 2 major, 1 major and 2 minor, or 3 minor manifestations, with evidence of preceding group A streptococcal infection.
results.title: Revision of the Jones Criteria for the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever in the era of Doppler echocardiography (Gewitz MH et al., Circulation 2015;131:1806-1818)

results.key_finding: Permanent pacing is indicated for third-degree or high-grade AV block and for Mobitz type II block once transient or reversible causes have been excluded. When a potentially reversible cause such as myocarditis is present, temporary pacing and observation are used before a permanent device.
results.title: 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and cardiac resynchronization therapy (Glikson M et al., Eur Heart J 2021;42:3427-3520)

results.key_finding: Secondary prophylaxis with benzathine penicillin G 1.2 million units intramuscularly every 4 weeks (every 3 weeks in high-risk settings). Duration after rheumatic fever with carditis and residual valvular disease: 10 years or until age 40, whichever is longer, sometimes lifelong.
results.title: Prevention of rheumatic fever and diagnosis and treatment of acute streptococcal pharyngitis: AHA scientific statement (Gerber MA et al., Circulation 2009;119:1541-1551)

output.summary: Jones 2015 defines recurrence criteria for rheumatic fever; ESC 2021 defers permanent pacing while a reversible cause such as myocarditis is treated; AHA 2009 sets benzathine penicillin secondary prophylaxis to at least age 40 after carditis with residual valve disease.

Stop chloroquine: it prolongs QT and impairs conduction; use mosquito-bite prevention, and a non-QT-prolonging agent if chemoprophylaxis is needed

Treat recurrent acute rheumatic fever with carditis (active inflammation with raised ESR, CRP and ASO): temporary transvenous pacing for recurrent high-grade block or pauses while the carditis is treated, with anti-inflammatory therapy

Benzathine penicillin G now to eradicate streptococci, then secondary prophylaxis every 3-4 weeks until at least age 40 (carditis with residual valve disease); the sulfonamide allergy is not a penicillin allergy
Permanent pacemaker if the high-grade AV block persists after the carditis settles (ESC 2021)
Echocardiographic follow-up of the mitral and aortic valve lesions and LV function

Tilt testing addresses reflex syncope; documented Mobitz II with bifascicular block establishes paroxysmal complete heart block from rheumatic carditis, and a tilt result would not change management.

Symptomatic Mobitz II with paroxysmal complete AV block is already a pacing indication; exercise testing adds risk without changing management of paroxysmal complete heart block from rheumatic carditis.

general.query: syncope initial evaluation and risk stratification

results.key_finding: Initial evaluation comprises history, physical examination including supine and standing blood pressure, and a 12-lead ECG. High-risk features (syncope during exertion or supine, palpitations before the event, known structural or coronary disease, family history of sudden death under 40, high-risk ECG findings) call for early in-hospital evaluation with immediate ECG monitoring. Echocardiography is indicated when structural heart disease is known or suspected; EEG, brain imaging and routine laboratory panels are not recommended without a specific indication.
results.title: 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope (Brignole M et al., Eur Heart J 2018;39:1883-1948)

results.key_finding: Risk stratification at the initial evaluation separates patients needing in-hospital monitoring and cardiac testing from those suitable for outpatient evaluation; targeted rather than routine blood testing is advised.
results.title: 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the evaluation and management of patients with syncope (Shen WK et al.)

general.summary: Guidelines base syncope work-up on the initial evaluation (history, examination, orthostatic BP, 12-lead ECG) and risk stratification; high-risk patients receive in-hospital ECG monitoring and targeted cardiac testing.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Amina Osei is a 21-year-old female university nursing student who presents to the emergency department after a witnessed episode of sudden loss of consciousness approximately 45 minutes ago. She was walking across the university campus with a classmate when she abruptly collapsed without any warning. Her classmate reports that after falling, Ms. Osei exhibited bilateral jerking of her arms and legs lasting approximately 8 to 10 seconds, followed by approximately 20 seconds of motionlessness and pallor. She then opened her eyes and was able to speak coherently within 30 seconds of the onset, asking what happened. She denied any aura, lightheadedness, chest pain, or palpitations preceding the event. There was no tongue biting or urinary incontinence. She was mildly confused for less than one minute before returning to her baseline mental status. This is her third such episode in the past two months. The first episode occurred six weeks ago while she was standing in line at the university cafeteria. She suddenly dropped to the floor without warning, and witnesses described brief shaking movements lasting only a few seconds. She recovered rapidly and attributed the episode to skipping breakfast that morning. The second episode occurred three weeks ago during a volleyball practice session. She collapsed during a sprint drill and was noted to be pale and briefly unresponsive for approximately 15 seconds before waking up confused for less than a minute. After this second event, she visited a local clinic where the physician suspected seizures and prescribed her a short course of diazepam, which she did not take regularly. She has also been experiencing progressive fatigue over the past four months, dyspnea on exertion, and intermittent palpitations, which she attributed to her anemia. She reports intermittent diffuse headaches, mild joint pain in her knees and elbows that she has had for several months, and occasional low-grade fevers. She has been living in a region endemic for malaria and other vector-borne illnesses and reports heavy mosquito exposure at her dormitory. She denies recent travel outside her university town, contact with sick persons, or exposure to animals. She has not had a formal cardiac evaluation and has no known cardiac history aside from her childhood rheumatic fever.
